summary.title: Testing Microservices, the sane way
summary.one_liner: Microservices are better tested by accepting that full end-to-end stacks on laptops are fragile and that pre-production tests are only a best-effort check, with production testing and monitoring covering the rest.
takeaways: Running the whole service topology on developer laptops is brittle and tends to amount to building a distributed monolith.
Testing is a spectrum: pre-production testing is a best-effort verification, and production techniques such as monitoring, feature flags, and shadowing complement it.
Choose testing and monitoring boundaries as part of system design, deciding what must be verified before production and what is better explored in production.
Exploratory testing is valuable for understanding a service, but the author argues it fits better in production than in pre-production testing.
Aim for testing that is reliable enough for the business's risk tolerance rather than trying to test everything.
summary.summary: The author, drawing on a failed attempt to run a full stack in a Vagrant box at a startup, argues that replicating an entire microservice topology locally is fragile and costly. He contends that teams should treat testing as a best-effort verification with a spectrum from pre-production to testing in production. The post draws on quotes from Sarah Mei, Tyler Treat, Fred Hébert, Charity Majors, the SRE book, and Lessons Learned in Software Testing. It is the first in a series on testing distributed systems and focuses on backend services.
